analysis.one_liner: Allows private student loans to be wiped out in bankruptcy like other debts.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in a House Judiciary subcommittee from March 2019 until the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, student loans can only be erased in bankruptcy if the borrower proves the payments are an 'undue hardship' — a very high bar that few people clear. This bill would change that for private student loans: lenders like banks and finance companies that issue education loans could no longer block borrowers from discharging those debts in bankruptcy. Loans made or guaranteed by the federal government would still be protected and would remain hard to erase.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers holding private student loans who end up in bankruptcy would be able to erase those debts the same way they can erase credit card and medical debt, instead of having to win an 'undue hardship' lawsuit against their lender. This mostly helps people whose loans came from private lenders rather than federal programs, and who face long-term financial distress.

how_it_helps.text: The bill removes private education loans from the bankruptcy code's list of debts that can only be discharged if the debtor proves undue hardship, letting them be wiped out like ordinary consumer debt.
It keeps the special protection only for loans made under federal programs or by institutions whose funds come substantially from the government, so federal student aid rules are untouched.
The change applies only to bankruptcy cases filed after enactment, so it would not reopen past cases.

analysis.who_pays: Private student loan lenders would bear the cost: some debts they currently can collect for decades would become dischargeable, and they would likely price that risk into future loans as higher interest rates or tighter credit standards. Bankruptcy filings could also rise among distressed borrowers seeking relief.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private student loan lenders and investors

drawbacks.text: Lenders would face higher expected losses on private student loans, which would likely be passed on to future borrowers as higher interest rates or stricter underwriting — the standard trade-off when a class of debt becomes dischargeable.

Because private lenders would no longer hold a legally protected claim, some borrowers with weak credit might find private student loans harder to get or more expensive, potentially pushing more students toward federal loans or away from borrowing altogether.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers drowning in private student debt, the benefit is direct and substantial: a realistic path out of unpayable loans instead of a near-impossible hardship standard. The cost is that private student credit would likely get more expensive, a trade-off supporters consider fair since these loans would simply be treated like every other consumer debt. The bill is narrow and targeted — it does not touch federal loans — so the downside is limited to the private lending market.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, then to its subcommittee on antitrust and commercial law in March 2019, and never moved again before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the bill on January 30, 2019, with ten original cosponsors, all Democrats.
It was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day it was introduced.
On March 25, 2019, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law, where no hearing, markup, or floor action followed.
The bill attracted 14 Democratic cosponsors in total and died at the end of the 116th Congress in January 2021 without ever receiving a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private student loan lenders and their investors, whose debts keep their special protected status and remain collectible even in bankruptcy. House leadership and the Judiciary Committee were spared a vote on a bill that had no recorded Republican support.

for.name: Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and secured ten original cosponsors.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat at the subcommittee level from March 2019 until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 14 cosponsors were Democrats and no votes were ever taken, so the House never recorded an opposition position; the bill's defeat came from inaction, not a roll call.

industries.note: The bill would strip these lenders of their special legal shield, allowing borrowers to erase private student loans in bankruptcy like credit card debt. Lenders would absorb some losses on existing loans and would likely charge more or lend less in the future.

industries.industry: Student loan debt collectors and servicers
industries.note: Debts that today survive bankruptcy and can be collected for decades would become dischargeable, shrinking the pool of long-lived collection accounts.
